headline: India says it does not endorse Hasina's remarks at New Delhi event
summary: The Indian government distances itself from statements made by deposed PM Sheikh Hasina during a private media event, as Bangladesh expresses strong disapproval.
details: India's Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the Indian government does not endorse any remarks made by deposed Bangladeshi PM Sheikh Hasina and other Awami League leaders at a media event in New Delhi on August 5.
The event, hosted by the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia, was a private media entity and the Indian government claimed it had no role in its organization.
During the event, Sheikh Hasina reiterated her plan to return to Bangladesh in December this year, despite being convicted by the International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity.
Bangladesh's foreign ministry issued a strong statement calling the interaction an 'affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh' and a 'grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution'.

Prime Minister’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir had previously sought New Delhi's cooperation to ensure that Indian territory is not used for political statements or activities aimed at creating instability in Bangladesh.
Bangladesh has sent letters to the Indian government seeking the extradition of Sheikh Hasina, but has received no response yet.
BNP and National Citizen Party leaders have also criticized the Indian government, accusing it of using Hasina as a tool to destabilize the country.
While bilateral relations have remained strained since the ouster of the Awami League government, there have been signs of improvement following the formation of the BNP government in February.
caption:
India distances itself from Sheikh Hasina's statements in New Delhi. Bangladesh calls it an 'affront to sovereignty'.

India's Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the Indian government does not endorse any remarks made by deposed Bangladeshi PM Sheikh Hasina and other Awami League leaders at a media event in New Delhi on August 5.

The event, hosted by the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia, was a private media entity and the Indian government claimed it had no role in its organization.

During the event, Sheikh Hasina reiterated her plan to return to Bangladesh in December this year, despite being convicted by the International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity.

Bangladesh's foreign ministry issued a strong statement calling the interaction an 'affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh' and a 'grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution'.

Prime Minister’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir had previously sought New Delhi's cooperation to ensure that Indian territory is not used for political statements or activities aimed at creating instability in Bangladesh.

Bangladesh has sent letters to the Indian government seeking the extradition of Sheikh Hasina, but has received no response yet.

BNP and National Citizen Party leaders have also criticized the Indian government, accusing it of using Hasina as a tool to destabilize the country.

While bilateral relations have remained strained since the ouster of the Awami League government, there have been signs of improvement following the formation of the BNP government in February.

headline_marked: 24% of children under five [[suffer from stunting]] in Bangladesh
headline: 24% of children under five suffer from stunting in Bangladesh
summary: A national survey reveals nearly one in four children are too short for their age due to chronic malnutrition, with the poorest households being twice as likely to be affected.
details: A national survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and Unicef found that 24 percent of children under five are moderately or severely stunted, meaning they are significantly shorter than WHO growth standards.

The data reveals sharp inequalities: children from the poorest households are more than twice as likely to be stunted (32.3%) compared to those from the richest (16.1%). Rural children and boys are also more affected.
While stunting rates have dropped from 59.6% in 1997 to 24% in 2025, Bangladesh remains in the WHO's 'high prevalence' category, ranking 49th highest globally for child stunting.

Stunting is a clear indicator of chronic malnutrition during the first 1,000 days of life. It impairs brain development, reduces cognitive ability, and increases vulnerability to respiratory and diarrhoeal diseases.
The long-term impact is severe: stunted children often enroll in school later, repeat grades, and as adults, earn about 20% less on average and are 30% more likely to live in poverty.

Roots of the problem begin before birth, with nearly half of Bangladeshi women marrying before 18 and one in four becoming pregnant during adolescence, increasing nutritional risks for both mother and baby.
The survey also found that two in three children aged 6-23 months do not consume enough food groups, with more than half being fed processed foods and one-third receiving no fruits or vegetables.
Public health experts call for greater investment in research, nationwide awareness campaigns on healthy feeding practices, and the restoration of school playgrounds to encourage physical activity.
caption:
Nearly one in four Bangladeshi children are too short for their age. Chronic malnutrition is stealing their physical and cognitive potential.

A national survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and Unicef found that 24 percent of children under five are moderately or severely stunted, meaning they are significantly shorter than WHO growth standards.

The data reveals sharp inequalities: children from the poorest households are more than twice as likely to be stunted (32.3%) compared to those from the richest (16.1%). Rural children and boys are also more affected.

While stunting rates have dropped from 59.6% in 1997 to 24% in 2025, Bangladesh remains in the WHO's 'high prevalence' category, ranking 49th highest globally for child stunting.

Stunting is a clear indicator of chronic malnutrition during the first 1,000 days of life. It impairs brain development, reduces cognitive ability, and increases vulnerability to respiratory and diarrhoeal diseases.

The long-term impact is severe: stunted children often enroll in school later, repeat grades, and as adults, earn about 20% less on average and are 30% more likely to live in poverty.

Roots of the problem begin before birth, with nearly half of Bangladeshi women marrying before 18 and one in four becoming pregnant during adolescence, increasing nutritional risks for both mother and baby.

The survey also found that two in three children aged 6-23 months do not consume enough food groups, with more than half being fed processed foods and one-third receiving no fruits or vegetables.

Public health experts call for greater investment in research, nationwide awareness campaigns on healthy feeding practices, and the restoration of school playgrounds to encourage physical activity.
